lessonTitle: Clinically Important Viruses: Hepatitis Viruses, Herpesviruses and HIV

blocks.text: A 74-year-old man develops a painful band of vesicles across one side of his forehead. He had chickenpox at the age of six and has felt entirely well since, yet the virus never left. How can a virus lie silent for decades and then return, and how can another virus quietly dismantle immunity until ordinary organisms become lethal?

blocks.markdown: This unit surveys four groups of viruses chosen because they illustrate **different strategies**: hepatitis viruses (differences in transmission and chronicity), herpesviruses (**latency** and **reactivation**), and the retrovirus HIV (progressive loss of CD4 T cells). Respiratory viruses such as influenza and respiratory syncytial virus, which cause acute self-limiting infection in most hosts, are the contrast case: they are cleared and do not establish latency.

blocks.title: Latency and reactivation
blocks.text: Latency is persistence of a viral genome in a host cell without production of infectious virus and with minimal viral gene expression, so the immune system does not eliminate it. Reactivation is the return to productive replication, usually triggered when immune control falls (illness, stress, immunosuppression, ageing).

blocks.caption: Hepatitis viruses compared
rows: Acute only; does not become chronic
Chronic in about 90% of infected neonates but about 5% of immunocompetent adults
Defective RNA virus; needs HBsAg to assemble
Chronic when co-infection or superinfection on chronic HBV
Usually acute; can be chronic in immunosuppressed; severe in pregnancy

blocks.markdown: **Why chronicity differs.** Hepatitis A and E are cleared by the immune response in most people and have no persistent reservoir in the liver. Hepatitis B persists when immune clearance is incomplete; the age of acquisition matters because the immature neonatal immune system tolerates the virus, so perinatal infection usually becomes chronic. Hepatitis C evades immunity through high genetic variability and often establishes chronic infection. **Chronic HBV and HCV infection** can lead to cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma. HDV cannot replicate without HBV, so HBV vaccination also prevents HDV.

blocks.title: Classifying a hepatitis presentation
blocks.prompt: A 26-year-old returns from an area with poor sanitation with jaundice. Serology shows IgM against a hepatitis virus and negative HBsAg and anti-HCV. Which virus group is most likely, what is its route, and what is the risk of chronicity?

steps.text: The exposure history (poor sanitation) points to faecal-oral transmission, shared by hepatitis A and E.
HBV and HCV are excluded by the negative serology, which fits an acute faecal-oral hepatitis.
HAV and HEV are both self-limited in a healthy adult; neither causes lifelong chronic infection in immunocompetent people.

blocks.answer: Hepatitis A (or E); faecal-oral route; acute illness with no chronicity in immunocompetent adults.

blocks.markdown: **Herpesviruses** are enveloped, double-stranded DNA viruses that establish **lifelong latent infection**. *Herpes simplex virus (HSV-1 and HSV-2)* is latent in **sensory ganglia** (trigeminal ganglion for orolabial disease, sacral ganglia for genital disease); reactivation produces recurrent vesicles at the supplied dermatome, triggered by fever, stress, ultraviolet light or immunosuppression. *Varicella-zoster virus (VZV)* causes chickenpox as primary infection and then lies latent in **dorsal root and cranial nerve ganglia**; reactivation causes **shingles**, a unilateral dermatomal vesicular rash that may be followed by post-herpetic neuralgia. *Cytomegalovirus* is latent in monocytes and other cells and reactivates in the immunosuppressed. *Epstein-Barr virus* is latent in B lymphocytes.

**HIV** is an enveloped RNA retrovirus. Glycoprotein gp120 binds the **CD4** receptor and a co-receptor (CCR5 or CXCR4), which targets CD4 T-helper cells, macrophages and dendritic cells. The enzyme **reverse transcriptase** copies the RNA genome into DNA, and **integrase** inserts it into the host genome as a provirus, which can remain latent. Viral replication and immune activation destroy CD4 T cells. Because CD4 T cells coordinate both cellular and humoral immunity, progressive loss leads to **acquired immunodeficiency**. When the CD4 count falls below about 200 cells/microlitre or an AIDS-defining illness occurs, the patient is said to have AIDS; opportunistic infections and tumours appear (for example *Pneumocystis jirovecii* pneumonia, cerebral toxoplasmosis, cryptococcal meningitis and Kaposi sarcoma).

blocks.title: Interpreting viral load change
blocks.prompt: A patient's HIV viral load falls from 200 000 copies/mL before treatment to 200 copies/mL after 12 weeks. By how many log10 units has it fallen, and by what factor?

steps.text: log10(1000) = 3, so the fall is 3 log10 units.

blocks.answer: A 3 log10 fall, which is a 1000-fold reduction.

blocks.caption: Strategies of persistence
rows: Dorsal root and cranial nerve ganglia

blocks.title: One principle
blocks.text: Chronic or latent viruses persist because they evade complete immune clearance, either by hiding (latency, integration) or by variation. Clinical disease appears when immune control weakens or when persistent infection causes cumulative damage.

blocks.title: Pitfalls
blocks.text: Do not state that all hepatitis viruses become chronic: HAV does not and HEV usually does not. Latency is not absence of infection. HIV causes AIDS through CD4 loss, but the infection is manageable once antiretroviral therapy suppresses viral replication.

points: HAV and HEV: faecal-oral, mainly acute; HBV, HCV, HDV: blood-borne; HBV and HCV cause chronic infection, with HBV risk highest at birth.
Herpesviruses establish lifelong latency (HSV in sensory ganglia, VZV in dorsal root ganglia) and reactivate when immunity falls.
HIV binds CD4 and a co-receptor, uses reverse transcriptase and integrase, and progressively depletes CD4 T cells, producing opportunistic disease.
Viral load changes are expressed in log10 units.

questions.stem: Which hepatitis virus is transmitted by the faecal-oral route and never causes chronic infection in an immunocompetent person?

options.text: Hepatitis A virus
Hepatitis B virus
Hepatitis C virus
Hepatitis D virus

distractorRationale.b: HBV is blood-borne and can become chronic.
distractorRationale.c: HCV is blood-borne and usually becomes chronic.
distractorRationale.d: HDV needs HBV and is transmitted by blood.

questions.explanation: HAV is transmitted by contaminated food and water and is cleared by the immune response, so it is acute only. The other viruses are blood-borne.

questions.stem: A newborn is infected with hepatitis B virus from her mother during delivery. Compared with an immunocompetent adult infected with the same virus, what is her risk of chronic infection?

options.text: Much higher, because the immature neonatal immune system tends to tolerate the virus
Much lower, because maternal antibody always clears HBV
The same, because age does not matter
Zero, because HBV is only transmitted sexually

questions.correctOptionText: Much higher, because the immature neonatal immune system tends to tolerate the virus

distractorRationale.b: Maternal transmission carries a high chronicity risk.
distractorRationale.c: Chronicity risk depends strongly on age at infection.
distractorRationale.d: HBV is also transmitted perinatally and by blood.

questions.explanation: Perinatal HBV infection becomes chronic in most cases, whereas most infected adults clear the virus. This is why neonatal prophylaxis and vaccination are important.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old man receiving chemotherapy has a painful unilateral band of grouped vesicles over the right lower back and flank, stopping at the midline. Which statement best explains the pathogenesis?

options.text: Reactivation of varicella-zoster virus latent in a dorsal root ganglion
Primary infection with herpes simplex virus type 2
Reactivation of hepatitis B virus
Direct spread of HIV from CD4 T cells to skin

questions.correctOptionText: Reactivation of varicella-zoster virus latent in a dorsal root ganglion

distractorRationale.d: HIV does not cause a dermatomal vesicular rash by direct spread.

questions.explanation: VZV remains latent in sensory ganglia after chickenpox and reactivates as immunity declines with age. Virus travels along the sensory nerve to the dermatome, producing the unilateral band.

questions.stem: Where does herpes simplex virus type 1 typically remain latent after an orolabial infection?

options.text: Trigeminal ganglion
Hepatocytes
CD4 T cells
Bone marrow plasma cells

distractorRationale.d: Plasma cells are not the HSV latency site.

questions.explanation: HSV travels along sensory neurons to the ganglion that supplies the infected site, which for orolabial disease is the trigeminal ganglion. Reactivation brings virus back down the nerve to cause recurrent lesions.

questions.stem: Which sequence best describes how HIV infection leads to immunodeficiency?

options.text: gp120 binds CD4 and a co-receptor; reverse transcription and integration occur; CD4 T cells are progressively depleted, impairing coordination of immunity
The virus binds B cells and prevents antibody class switching only
The virus integrates into neutrophils and inhibits phagocytosis
The virus destroys red blood cells and so lowers oxygen delivery

questions.correctOptionText: gp120 binds CD4 and a co-receptor; reverse transcription and integration occur; CD4 T cells are progressively depleted, impairing coordination of immunity

distractorRationale.b: The principal target is the CD4 T cell, not B cells alone.
distractorRationale.c: Neutrophils are not the main target.
distractorRationale.d: HIV does not primarily destroy red cells.

questions.explanation: CD4 T-helper cells are needed to coordinate both cell-mediated and antibody responses. As they are depleted, opportunistic infections and tumours emerge.

questions.stem: A patient on antiretroviral therapy has an HIV viral load of 80 000 copies/mL at baseline and 80 copies/mL at 12 weeks. By how many log10 units has the viral load fallen?
questions.explanation: The fold change is 80 000 / 80 = 1000, and log10(1000) = 3. A fall of 3 log10 units therefore corresponds to a 1000-fold reduction in circulating virus.

questions.stem: An untreated patient has a CD4 count of 560 cells/microlitre and it falls steadily by 60 cells/microlitre per year. Assuming a constant rate, how many years until the count reaches 200 cells/microlitre, the AIDS threshold used in the lesson?
questions.explanation: The total fall needed is 560 - 200 = 360 cells/microlitre. At 60 cells/microlitre per year this takes 360 / 60 = 6 years, an illustration of progressive loss (real decline varies between individuals).

questions.stem: Compare hepatitis A, B and C viruses in terms of route of transmission and risk of chronic infection, explaining why hepatitis A does not become chronic.
markingGuide: HBV: blood, sexual, perinatal; chronic in most perinatally infected neonates and a small percentage of adults
HCV: blood; chronic in the majority
HAV is cleared by the immune response without a persistent reservoir
HBV and HCV chronicity risks hepatic cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma
questions.explanation: Route and chronicity differ among hepatitis viruses and determine prevention strategy. Persistence needs a mechanism, such as integration or immune evasion, which HAV lacks.

questions.stem: Explain what is meant by latency and reactivation in herpesvirus infection, using varicella-zoster virus as the example.
markingGuide: Virus becomes latent in dorsal root or cranial nerve ganglia
Latency means genome persists without infectious virus production and escapes immune clearance
Reactivation when cell-mediated immunity declines (age, immunosuppression, stress)
Virus travels along sensory nerve causing dermatomal vesicular rash (shingles), possibly post-herpetic neuralgia
questions.explanation: Latency is persistence without replication, and reactivation is return to productive infection. VZV illustrates both in the same patient decades apart.

questions.stem: Explain how HIV infection leads to progressive immunodeficiency and give two opportunistic infections that mark advanced disease.
markingGuide: gp120 binds CD4 and a co-receptor (CCR5 or CXCR4) on CD4 T cells, macrophages and dendritic cells
Reverse transcriptase makes DNA from RNA genome; integrase inserts provirus
Viral replication and immune activation deplete CD4 T cells over time
CD4 T cells coordinate cell-mediated and humoral immunity so loss impairs both
Opportunistic infections such as Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia, cerebral toxoplasmosis or cryptococcal meningitis
AIDS considered when CD4 falls below about 200 cells/microlitre or an AIDS-defining illness occurs
questions.explanation: HIV targets the cells that coordinate immunity and so produces a gradual loss of defences. Opportunistic organisms that healthy immunity controls then cause disease.
